source: Wang and Xu (2026) AllocBench: Measuring Online Tool Allocation Capability in LLM Agents
finding: Gap 1 and 2. Frontier models know how to wait for a task to repeat before paying to build a tool, but only when the choice is posed in the abstract. When the same choice means writing a reusable script, they build on the first instance almost every time.
numbers: Streams of T=60 numeric problems from 8 families (3 hot families hold 0.85 of the mass, 5 traps). Tool budget B per session. 24 paired seeds per model. First-sight commitment rate by rung R0 / R1 / R2 / R3: Haiku 4.5 28/33/99/100%; Opus 4.8 4/0/92/99%; GPT-5.4-mini 15/29/85/88%; GPT-5.6 Sol 24/0/39/100%. In the abstract rung every model waits for recurrence more than 70% of the time; in R3 none waits more than 12% of the time.
quote: every frontier model we test ... acts near-optimally in the abstract framing but fails to transfer this ability to script-writing
limits: Single group, preprint (31 Jul 2026 v2). Tool payoff in R2 does not depend on code correctness. Cost of building is a budget count, not tokens. Reasoning effort held fixed within model, not varied.
agent_relevance: Making a tool is an investment decision. A scaffold should have an explicit 'has this task type recurred?' gate before building, because models skip that reasoning once they are in code-writing mode.

source: Wang and Xu (2026) AllocBench, post-training on abstract allocation (Section 4.4, Table 2)
finding: A small open model (Qwen2.5-Coder-14B) was trained with PPO to wait in the abstract game. The skill did not carry over to tool making.
numbers: R0 first-sight commitment fell from 74% to 6% after 20 steps of 25 episodes. Score (percent of hindsight-optimal utility) R0 / R1 / R2: base 74.8 / 49.2 / 61.2; post-trained 79.6 / 34.8 / 41.7. At R1 (numeric problems, declarative keep/pass) base and trained are statistically indistinguishable on first-sight commitment.
limits: One training attempt, one 14B model. Authors say the R2 drop reflects a code-emission limit of the 14B model.
agent_relevance: A prompt or rule that teaches budget discipline in one frame may not hold when the same decision appears inside a coding task. Put the gate in the schema state, not in the model's habits.

source: AllocBench related-work claims: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz and Si (2024) Library learning doesn't; Liu et al. (2025) Budget-Aware Tool-Use
finding: Second-hand (read in the AllocBench related-work section, primary papers not opened). AllocBench states that library-learning methods give much less reuse than expected and mostly improve through self-correction. It also says a larger tool-call budget does not help web-search agents that lack budget awareness.
numbers: No numbers given in AllocBench for these two claims.
limits: Primary papers could not be retrieved this session (search APIs rate-limited). Treat as a lead, not as evidence.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 lead: part of a library's gain may come from the extra execute-and-repair pass, not from reuse. A test should separate 'tool is reused' from 'tool was verified by running'.

source: Chen et al. (2026) SkillCraft (Table 3 re-read for token accounting)
finding: Gap 1 (partly closed for in-task reuse). In SkillCraft the agent writes its own skills inside the same task run, so the token count includes the cost of making them. Skill mode still cut tokens sharply with current models.
numbers: Per task, 126 tasks. GPT-5.2: success 109 to 114 of 126 (87 to 90%), tokens 1.23M to 0.26M (-79%), cost $1.77 to $0.43, turns 20.6 to 9.9. Claude 4.5 Sonnet: 119 to 121 of 126, tokens 1.36M to 0.40M (-71%). Gemini 3 Pro: 108 to 116, tokens 0.66M to 0.30M (-54%). DeepSeek-V3.2: 76 to 87, 1.04M to 0.53M (-49%). Minimax-M2.1: 117 to 119, only -11% tokens. Limits: 1M input and 150K output tokens per task, temperature 0.
limits: Reuse is inside one task family and often inside one run (several entities per task), not held-out items across a stream. The base arm is a plain tool-calling agent, not a reasoning-token-matched baseline. Not a LATM-style maker/user split.
agent_relevance: Evidence that make-then-reuse can win at charged cost on repeated sub-calls with current models. It does not show a win on single non-repeating problems.

source: Chen et al. (2026) SkillCraft: hierarchical (nested) skills versus flat skills (Table 3, Section 5)
finding: Gap 5. Nested skills are not worse everywhere even inside SkillCraft. The result depends on the model.
numbers: Success N of 126, Base / flat Skill / Hierarchy: DeepSeek-V3.2 76 / 87 / 92 (hierarchy better, reuse 3.0x vs 4.8x); Claude 4.5 Sonnet 119 / 121 / 121 (equal, but tokens 0.63M vs 0.40M, cost $0.44 vs $0.28); GPT-5.2 109 / 114 / 100 (hierarchy worse, 90% to 79%, tokens 0.60M vs 0.26M). Authors list three causes: compounding failure with depth, latent bugs in early skills, debugging cost. Hierarchy often has 95 to 99% execution success yet lower task success.
quote: shallow, well-tested skill libraries are currently more reliable
limits: Max nesting depth 10 in the harness. One benchmark. The headline '90% to 79%' in claim K15 is the GPT-5.2 row only.
agent_relevance: Flat, well-tested skills are the safe default. Nested composition costs more tokens in all three models shown (DeepSeek 0.68M vs 0.53M) and helps task success in only one.

source: Chen et al. (2026) SkillCraft: cross-task transfer and cross-model skill quality (Table 4, Figure 7)
finding: Gap 3 (partly). Skills written by a strong model and handed to others lift success and cut tokens; skills of low quality can cost tokens. Transferred skills ran with 97 to 100% execution success.
numbers: Claude 4.5 Sonnet easy-to-hard transfer: success 95 to 100%, tokens 1.92M to 1.56M; hard-to-hard: 95% kept, tokens 1.96M to 0.47M. Gemini 3 Pro easy-to-hard: 76 to 90%, tokens 1.33M to 0.78M; hard-to-hard: 76 to 100%, 1.30M to 0.75M. Figure 7 heatmap shows negative token savings (values near -45 and -48) in some cells where skills from weaker creators (GLM, Minimax) were used.
limits: Heatmap cell mapping not fully recovered from the text extraction. Transfer is static (no accumulation in phase 2). Does not separate storage-time testing from the library itself.
agent_relevance: Library value depends on who made the tool and whether it was tested. Store only tools that pass tests, and track per-tool pass rate.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager, ablation section 3.4 (re-read for gap 3)
finding: Gap 3 stays open. Voyager removes self-verification as a whole feedback type, which also controls when to move to the next task. That mixes 'only store verified skills' with 'decide when to stop'. The library ablation is reported as a plateau, with no number in the text.
numbers: Random curriculum: discovered items -93%. No self-verification: -73%. GPT-3.5 instead of GPT-4 for code: GPT-4 gets 5.7x more unique items. Library removal: 'tendency to plateau in the later stages' (figure only).
quote: Self-verification is the most important among all the feedback types.
limits: Minecraft, GPT-4 era, N small. Verification gates both storage and progression, so the two effects are confounded.
agent_relevance: No study yet isolates verify-before-store at equal tokens. Our own test must hold the library fixed and toggle the test-before-store step.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad and Bansal (2024) ReGAL: refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions (ablation Table 3)
finding: Gap 3 and 4. A library learned by refactoring with execution checks helps open models; removing the later quality steps (edit, prune, retry) each cost accuracy. This is the closest published ablation of what happens to a stored tool after it passes the first test.
numbers: CodeLlama-13B dev splits, 3 seeds, LOGO / Date / TextCraft: full 55.0 / 77.0 / 34.12; no retry 48.3 / 51.9 / 30.43; no curriculum 36.3 / 56.6 / 28.78; no pruneCodeBank 52.0 / 65.5 / 25.26; no editCodeBank 53.3 / 69.6 / 27.35. CodeLlama-13B with ReGAL beats GPT-3.5 without abstractions by 19.2 points (as stated in the text).
limits: Training cost (GPT-3.5 refactoring over about 200 examples) is not counted against the test agent. The verify step itself is not ablated (it defines what enters the library). A ReAct 'think about which functions' prompt was needed or the agent rarely used helpers.
agent_relevance: Keep an edit and prune cycle on the library. Prompt the agent to name which tools may apply before it writes code.

source: Stengel-Eskin et al. (2024) ReGAL: distribution shift on TextCraft (Section 5)
finding: Gap 4. Under a shift to unseen target objects, pruning the old library alone gave a gain, and re-learning on new data gave more.
numbers: Train/dev/test 100/20/76 instances. ReGAL beats the primitive-only agent by 3.6 points under shift. Pruning only: a further +3.5. One more training pass with new abstractions and edits: a further +2.3, total +9.4 over baseline.
limits: One environment, small test set (76). Open models.
agent_relevance: Pruning is not only a size control. It is a way to adapt a library when the task mix changes.

source: Wang, Neubig and Fried (2024) TroVE, full text re-read: INSTANCE baseline and trimming ablation
finding: Gap 4. A library with no reuse control hurts. TroVE's own INSTANCE baseline (a new function per example) produced hundreds to thousands of functions and scored below primitives-only on most table datasets. Trimming cuts library size 74-90% with only a small accuracy change. The abstract's '79-98% smaller' is versus other methods, not versus its own no-trim run.
numbers: CodeLlama-7B. GQA: INSTANCE created 395 functions and fell 0.21 below PRIMITIVE. TroVE vs INSTANCE: 8.7 to 83.3% higher correctness with 60.0 to 90.2% fewer tools. TroVE vs PRIMITIVE: +30 to 120% correctness on 7 MATH datasets. Trimming ablation (Table 8): library size down 74-90%; the text says accuracy and complexity 'slightly degraded' with trimming. Per-cell values (MATH algebra 0.25, HiTab 0.15/0.18, GQA 0.39/0.44) are garbled in the PDF text and not used.
quote: confusing the model with too many low-utility options
limits: Table 8 row alignment not recoverable from PDF text. Authors blame 'too many low-utility options' for INSTANCE, not measured separately. 7B open model, not a frontier model.
agent_relevance: Library size hurts when the agent sees every tool. Add a trim step, but expect a small accuracy price on some tasks.

source: Wang et al. (2024) TroVE vs LATM, CREATOR, CRAFT with GPT-4 (Table 3)
finding: Gap 4. Library size in other published systems is 10 to 500 times larger than TroVE's, with similar accuracy. TroVE does not win everywhere.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy (library size) algebra / TabMWP / GQA: LATM 0.30 / 0.09 / 0.29 (no library count); CRAFT 0.68 (282) / 0.88 (181) / 0.45 (525); CREATOR 0.65 (875) / 0.81 (4,595) / 0.34; TROVE 0.72 (16) / 0.92 (38) / 0.44 (8).
limits: Baseline numbers are copied from the CRAFT paper, not rerun. CRAFT 0.45 is above TroVE 0.44 on GQA, so 'best on all' is not exact. Row alignment read from PDF text.
agent_relevance: A small curated library can match a large one on accuracy; the smaller one costs less context.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) CRAFT: toolset size sweep (Section 4.4)
finding: Gap 4. With multi-view retrieval, accuracy rose with library size up to 525 tools, with the biggest jump from none to 261. This conflicts with TroVE's INSTANCE result unless retrieval and de-duplication decide the outcome.
numbers: Toolsets of 0, 261, 337 and 525 tools on GQA, OK-VQA and A-OKVQA with GPT-3.5: soft accuracy rises in all three at each step. No point shows a decline.
limits: Only three sizes, none above 525, so no turn-over point is tested. Retrieval returns a few tools into the prompt, so context cost stays flat. The reconciliation (retrieval makes size safe) is my inference, not tested by either paper.
agent_relevance: Large libraries are safe only behind retrieval. Test growth beyond 525 on a modern model with a token cap.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) CRAFT: abstraction ablation (Section 4.1, Table 3)
finding: Gap 3 and 8. Abstracting a one-off solution into a general, named function is worth a lot. Without it the library barely beats the no-tool baseline.
numbers: GPT-3.5 on GQA soft accuracy: ViperGPT 35.0; CRAFT 45.4; abstraction removed about 37.1 (row mapping read from PDF text; the paper says the abstraction-ablated version still beats ViperGPT across all three datasets). Removing function names costs more than 6.6 absolute points.
limits: Row labels in the text extraction are misaligned, so the 37.1 figure carries mild uncertainty.
agent_relevance: A tool template should force a general signature, a name and a docstring. Name quality drives retrieval.

source: Qian et al. (2023) CREATOR: tool-creation hints (Table 4, Creation Challenge, ChatGPT)
finding: Gap 8 (partial). Giving the maker a spec for the tool (what it is for, plus its inputs and outputs) lifted accuracy by about 12 points. A tool interface helps more than free-form making. This is not a test of fixed reusable templates.
numbers: Creation Challenge accuracy: CREATOR no hint 63.8, utility hint 67.2, all hint (utility plus input and output) 75.7. Entangled variant 64.5 / 65.8 / 75.3. Baselines: PoT with rectification 61.1 (no CoT), Standard 27.9.
limits: Hints are human written per item, so this is a human-supplied spec, not the model's own template. ChatGPT, 2023.
agent_relevance: If the schema fixes the tool interface (name, purpose, inputs, outputs) before code is written, expect a gain. Whether a fixed library of templates beats free-form making has not been tested.

source: Klein-Seetharaman et al. (2026) Lomekwi: tool-prior prompt recovers recognition (Section 6.4)
finding: Gap 2 (partly closed). The size inversion in tool recognition is mostly a matter of not bothering to look. Telling the model that exactly one of the tools can solve the task brings back exploration and the largest models recover.
numbers: Recognition = P(oracle tool found). Qwen3.5 27B 0.02 to 0.60 (tool calls 0.2 to 5.6 per episode); Qwen2.5 32B 0.15 to 0.89; Qwen3 32B 0.06 to 0.85. Qwen3.5 curve under prior: 0.42, 0.28, 0.24, 0.60 for 2B, 4B, 9B, 27B (U-shape). Baseline Qwen3.5: 0.29, 0.10, 0.05, 0.02.
quote: the largest models return to exploring the tools and their recognition recovers
limits: Qwen only, thinking disabled ('/no think'), under 35B parameters. Claude models not run in this recovery test. A hint that a tool exists is also a spoiler, so it is a different task from open recognition.
agent_relevance: A schema step that states 'a helper tool may exist; check the tool list' is a cheap fix for under-using tools, and it should be tested on current models.

source: Klein-Seetharaman et al. (2026) Lomekwi: Claude models and two-step tool depth (Section 4, Appendix)
finding: Gap 2 (partly). The inversion also shows up in Claude. Opus builds less than Haiku. With a two-level tool (build a supershard, then a machine) the first step shows the inversion and the second step is flat.
numbers: Models: claude-haiku-4-5, claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-opus-4-8; 180 episodes per model, 9 configurations. Opus 'builds less than Haiku'. Depth experiment: first step P(build supershard | both shards) is much lower for Sonnet and Opus than Haiku; second step is flat across size. Exact Claude values are in figures only.
limits: No extended-thinking setting is reported for Claude; the prompt says 'Think briefly'. So the question 'does extended thinking fix it' is still untested. Single group.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a stronger model will reach for tools. The scaffold should put a tool check before hand solving.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver, Appendix C: effect of self-reflection by model
finding: Gap 6 (partly). Step-wise self-reflection helped only GPT-4. It did not reduce infeasible answers for the two weaker models tested (Claude2 and Llama2-13b), and Llama2 always declared its first answer wrong. Divergent-convergent prompting helped all models.
numbers: Models: GPT-4, Claude2, Llama2-13b. GPT-4 base: 37.5% infeasible, 18.9% efficient. Reflection: GPT-4 infeasible down 9.7 points (earlier evidence b21). Divergent-convergent raised efficient answers by 6.5 points for GPT-4.
limits: Models are 2023 era. No equal-token control: reflection adds a second pass. No current reasoning model was found tested on MacGyver. The two weaker models are named from the paper's model list; the appendix sentence says 'these two models'.
agent_relevance: A feasibility check helps only if the checker can really judge physics. Keep it conditional on a capable model.

source: von Bayern, Danel, Auersperg, Mioduszewska and Kacelnik (2018) Compound tool construction by New Caledonian crows (full text re-read)
finding: Gap 9 closed. The need-discrimination figures and the Fisher p values are in the paper text and match evidence line b07.
numbers: 4 of 8 crows built a compound tool in construction test 1, within about 4 to 6 minutes of interacting with the parts. Unrewarded attempts before success: Tumulte 0, Tabou 3, Mango 7, Jungle 10. Need test (4 birds): tried an uncombined tool first on 70.8% of close-food trials and 20.8% of distant-food trials, so they built compounds at once on 79.2% of the cases where needed. Fisher exact per bird: Jungle p=0.037, Tumulte p=0.001, Tabou p=0.100, Mango p=0.193 (2 of 4 reach p<0.05). Inter-rater r=0.993. Tests: up to 6 trials of up to 12 min; replication until 3 successes or 6 failures.
quote: Our results are not accountable by direct reinforcement learning
limits: Only the 4 successful birds reached the need test, so no group test; the other 4 birds hardly combined. Birds had earlier experience with 15 cm dowels. Wild-caught, history unknown.
agent_relevance: Building on demand when a short tool fails is the model for a tool-make gate: try the cheap option when reach is near, build when far.

source: Chappell and Kacelnik (2004) Selection of tool diameter by New Caledonian crows (abstract, summarising the 2002 length study)
finding: Gap 9 (partly). Abstract opened via Europe PMC; the 2002 tool-selection primary paper was not retrievable (not on Europe PMC, guessed publisher link returned 404). The 2004 paper reports preference for the thinnest of three loose sticks, a bundle taken apart only when the preferred stick was tied, and a branch made and trimmed to fit a hole.
numbers: No sample sizes or percentages in the abstract. Experiment 1: three loose sticks, thinnest preferred. Experiment 2: tool made and modified during use to match the hole's diameter.
limits: Abstract only; the 2002 length-selection numbers remain unverified here (b18 and a18 stay opened:false).
agent_relevance: Selecting among made options by the task's property (length, width) is the template-and-fit step our library needs.

source: Search log for gaps 6, 7 and 8 (Europe PMC queries, 2026-11-03; arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate-limited)
finding: Gap 7: three Europe PMC queries combining LLM terms with crow, corvid, Aesop, tool innovation and animal cognition returned no study that runs LLMs on crow-style tasks (compound tools, out-of-sight metatool stages, Aesop's fable) with a first-trial versus learned-success null model. The one on-topic hit was Yiu, Kosoy and Gopnik (already in c13). Gap 6: no current-model MacGyver reflection study was found. Gap 8: no fixed-template versus free-form tool-making comparison was found.
numbers: Count of on-topic hits: 1 (already known) in about 40 listed results. WebSearch budget was already used up by other agents after one query.
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search. arXiv listing and citation graphs could not be queried this run. Europe PMC covers few computer-science preprints.
agent_relevance: These three questions are open: they are good tests for our own harness.
